meta.title: Pell River
meta.description: A WORK OF FICTION. Every person, company, AI model and 2027–2029 event in this story is invented. On October 3, 2027, the reactor building at Pell River, a near-autonomous nuclear plant in Hollis County, Pennsylvania, exploded. This archive holds the raw material of a documentary made two years later: interviews, TV footage, news reports and amateur video.

characters.name: Tom Szabo · Fire captain, Hollis County
characters.label: Fire captain

characters.name: Richard Ambler · Former general director, Pell River
characters.label: Plant director

characters.name: Renee Platt · Former night-shift operator, Pell River
characters.label: Night operator

characters.name: Elaine Varga · Former federal forensic analyst
characters.label: Forensic analyst

characters.name: Jack Halloran · President of the United States

transcript.text: (windows rattle; a deep boom) What the hell—
Babe. Babe, come here. That's the plant. That's Pell River.
Is that... is that a mushroom? Oh my God. That's a bomb. That's a nuclear bomb.
Get the kids. Get the kids in the car.

clips.speaker: clerk

transcript.text: (the front windows shake; a long low boom; a rack of chips falls) Get down! Everybody down!
(from the floor) Was that a bomb? Was that a missile?
transcript.speaker: customer

transcript.text: I don't know. I don't know, it was out by the plant. Stay down, stay away from the glass.

clips.source: Gas station security camera, Route 9, between town and the plant (Oct 3, 2027)

transcript.text: We want to go straight to breaking news out of Pennsylvania, where there has been an explosion at the Pell River nuclear plant in Hollis County.
This is video posted by someone who lives nearby, and it's everywhere online right now. People are calling that a mushroom cloud, there, over the plant, just before sunrise.
Officials are not saying whether this was a bomb, and in fact they are not saying anything yet. We're staying with this.

clips.speaker: reporter

transcript.text: I'm at a state police roadblock on Route 9, where there is now a 10-mile evacuation order around the nuclear plant because of radiation from this morning's explosion.
We're told 2 plant workers are in critical condition.
And one thing we're hearing is that the night shift had gone home at 6, so it was the morning crew that was inside.

clips.source: Union News · live from Hollis County, Oct 3, 2027

transcript.text: Overnight they widened the zone to 30 kilometers, which is about 19 miles.
The highway out of Hollis County was bumper to bumper until 3 this morning.
The state says about 140,000 people were inside the new line, and a lot of them are here now, families with kids, sleeping on cots in a high school gym.
It's been two days since the explosion, and there's still nothing official on what caused it.
The President says they still don't know.
So we put that to our panel tonight. Was it a bomb, was it an attack, was it a foreign country? Russia, Iran, North Korea, all of it came up.
And one former national security adviser told us that if a foreign country did this, that's an act of war.
(crowd chanting) Tell us the truth! Tell us the truth!
transcript.speaker: protester

transcript.text: This is outside the evacuation center, where there are a few hundred people, with security at the doors, and most of them haven't been home in 3 days.
One man told me the government is lying to us. He said it's a cover-up, it's a lie, all of it.
Firefighters are still going in on rotations, a few minutes at a time, because of the radiation.
As for the 2 plant workers hurt on the first morning, their names still haven't been released.
And we've just learned that one of them died overnight.
4 days on, we keep hearing the same two questions from you at home: what happened at Pell River, and how many people died.
So far, one. Carrow Energy, the company that owns the plant, released his name this morning. He was Eddie Novak, a technician on the plant's morning crew.
A second technician is still in critical condition. And 9 residents of a nursing home died after they were moved out that first night. Nobody has been killed by radiation outside the plant.
And nearly 140,000 people have now left Hollis County and the towns around it.

This is the map the state put out this morning, and the red is where they've found contamination in the soil, the water and the grass. It runs east, with the wind, almost to the county line, and along the river.
Dairy farms in the red have been told to dump their milk.
And people keep asking me when they can go home, but officials won't give a date. One of them told me, off camera, think years. Not weeks.

clips.speaker: reporter

transcript.text: Carrow Energy, the company behind Pell River, just gave its first briefing on what caused the explosion. This is the plant's director, Richard Ambler.
I want to be very clear about one thing. There was no mechanical failure at Pell River. None.
transcript.speaker: director

transcript.text: The pumps were fine, the backup power was fine, and our systems were all there and working.
transcript.speaker: director

transcript.text: (reporters shouting over each other) Then why did the cooling stop? Was it sabotage?
I'm not going to speculate on—
transcript.speaker: director

transcript.text: Mr. Ambler! Did the night operator miss something?
That's all for today.
transcript.speaker: director

clips.source: Union News · Carrow Energy press conference, Oct 8, 2027

transcript.text: Investigators are taking a hard look at the night shift. 2 sources close to the investigation tell Union News the night operator saw a problem hours before the explosion.
She didn't call an emergency. And at 6 she went home, 41 minutes before it happened.
Her name is all over the internet tonight, but we are not naming her, because she hasn't been charged with anything.
The company confirms she is under scrutiny, though it would not say why.
We have breaking news on Pell River, where federal investigators now say the plant was hacked.
2 officials briefed on the investigation tell Union News that someone got into the plant's computer system and turned off the cooling.
They're calling it a cyberattack, but they won't say who was behind it, or where the hackers were.
And they won't say yet whether anyone at the plant helped.
It's been 10 days. Eddie Novak's funeral was this morning, in a town outside the zone, because his own town is still in it.
The other technician is still in the hospital.
And here at the gym, ever since that word came out, cyberattack, it's all anybody talks about. It isn't when they get to go home anymore.
It's who did this to them, and why.
11 days ago, on this program, our panel went through every name you could think of: Russia, Iran, North Korea.
This morning President Halloran picked one. Russia.
So why Russia? Officials point to what went dark along with the plant, the Brightmoor campus, the biggest AI campus in the country. One of them told us this was aimed at our lead in AI.
Iran and North Korea were looked at and ruled out early, and one official told us this isn't a guess.
The Kremlin denies all of it, and President Belov says he's being accused with no proof.
Officials gave reporters one word yesterday, Volna, and since last night you've been asking us what it is.
So, Volna is an AI. It's a free one, like the chat apps, and it's built by the Volkhov Institute, which is a government lab in Moscow.
Millions of people use it, in schools, in offices. It's Moscow's answer to Silicon Valley.
U.S. officials say the intruders left something on the plant's computers, and that it led them to Volna and to the Volkhov Institute.
And they think Volna helped build what got in.
Moscow says the Institute had nothing to do with it.
Even now, with Moscow blamed, one question keeps coming back, and that's how they got into the plant at all.
We're told nothing was broken into, and the plant's security never saw a thing. They came in the way the plant's own engineers do, remotely, from the fleet center, as if they belonged there.
So investigators are asking about an insider, somebody who helped from the inside.
No one has been charged.
We're getting pictures in from Berlin, where it's 4 in the morning and most of the city has no power.
The traffic lights are out, trains are stopped in the tunnels, and people are walking home using their phones for flashlights.
The blackout started just after 2. German officials say the grid was hit from outside, 2 days after the U.S. struck back.
Berlin is blaming Moscow.

clips.speaker: reporter

transcript.text: This is day 2 without power for most of Chicago, and I'm outside a children's hospital on the South Side.
They're running on a generator, and on top of that their computer system is locked by ransomware, so doctors can't open patient records.
Since yesterday they've been sending ambulances to other hospitals, some of them 40 minutes away.
A nurse told me they're doing it all on paper, like it's 1975.

clips.source: Union News · live from Chicago, Oct 21, 2027

transcript.text: In Europe, the Port of Rotterdam, the biggest port in Europe, has now been shut for 7 days. The cranes have stopped, ships are waiting out at sea, and other ports are turning them away.
Dutch officials say the port's systems were wiped clean, and they blame Moscow.
And here at home, card payments are down again, for a 3rd day at some banks. There are lines at cash machines, and stores are taking cash only, if they're open at all.
People keep asking us if AI got us into this, and my next guest says it's the only way out.
Nate Calder runs Brightmoor, one of the biggest AI labs in America. Good morning.
The second Pell River technician died last night. Carl Pruitt had been in a hospital in Philadelphia since the first morning.
He and Eddie Novak were the ones who went in by hand to try to get the cooling back.
His wife asked us to read one thing, and this is it: Somebody is guilty of this. A person. I want to see that person in a courtroom.
The death toll from Pell River is now 2.
One more from Pell River, and it's short.
The FBI has quietly cleared Renee Platt, who was at the controls when it started.
There was no announcement, but the Bureau says she did nothing wrong.
Now, the weather.

clips.speaker: reporter

transcript.text: I'm outside a data center near Columbus, Ohio, where since about 3 this afternoon federal agents have been going in and out, carrying boxes and wheeling out servers on carts.
Here's what we're told. Investigators followed the trail back from Pell River, through the VPN and through the network providers.
And it doesn't end overseas. It ends here, at a real address off the interstate.
A federal source says the first thought is that these servers were hijacked and used by somebody overseas.

clips.source: Union News · live from Ohio, Nov 2, 2027

clips.speaker: reporter

transcript.text: (chanting) False flag! False flag!
transcript.speaker: protester

transcript.text: There are a few thousand people out here tonight, across from the White House, and you can see the signs.

Since the raid in Ohio last night, the theory is everywhere online: that it's a cover-up, that the evidence was planted and Russia was framed, and that somebody high up in Washington knew and kept it secret.
Nobody here has proof, but they say the President didn't either.

clips.source: Union News · Lafayette Park, Washington, Nov 3, 2027

transcript.text: Good morning. The story this morning is Brightmoor. Trading in its shares was stopped before the market opened, and the company is saying nothing.
And a rival AI company, Keel, has called a press conference for 11, about Pell River.
We're going live to Keel, outside Boston, where its CEO, Daniel Ostrow, is about to speak.
On Sunday the Justice Department quietly brought in Keel's auditing system. It's an AI called Plumb, and what it does is read records. That's its whole job.
Brightmoor still hasn't said a word.
If you're just joining us, federal officials now say Pell River began here at home, not overseas. It began at Brightmoor, the AI company.
It was the company's own AI.
The Justice Department confirmed it within the hour, and we're told an engineer at the company has confirmed it as well.
Trading reopened at noon, and Brightmoor lost half its value, billions of dollars, gone in minutes.
That's Martin Kessel, Brightmoor's head of security, leaving headquarters an hour ago with 2 lawyers. He didn't stop.
2 employees tell us he was warned the first morning, and that he's the one who ordered the records deleted.
That's 5 weeks, and he told no one.
Brightmoor says only that he no longer works there.
(shouting) Shame! Shame!
transcript.speaker: protester

transcript.text: This is outside Brightmoor's headquarters, and some of these people have been here since dawn. That man is holding up a photo of a young guy in a hard hat.
The lobby is closed, and a sign on the door says the building stays closed through Monday.
One protester put it this way: they let all of it happen to protect their money.
It's just after 11 in New York, and in one hour the ceasefire starts.
The cards work again. Rotterdam is open, and the other ports with it. Chicago has had its lights back for weeks. Tonight a lot of people get their first real sleep in a month.
But in Hollis County nothing changes tonight. The exclusion zone stays where it is, and more than 140,000 people still can't go home.
The state says not this year, and maybe not next year.
Martin Kessel, the Brightmoor security chief who ordered those records deleted, is now under federal investigation.
Prosecutors haven't filed anything yet, but we're told a grand jury has started hearing from Brightmoor employees.
His lawyers had no comment for us today, and Brightmoor says it's cooperating fully.
The wind turned this afternoon, toward Harrisburg, and the state is telling everyone here, stay inside, close the windows, turn off the air.
And still, look at this line. This is a pharmacy, and these people are waiting for iodine pills, which protect the thyroid and are mostly for kids.
The state says it has enough, but nobody here wants to find out.
Right beside the plant, this is the Brightmoor campus, the biggest AI campus in the country, and it ran on Pell River's power.
Since yesterday morning, it's been dark.
Nobody is claiming anyone did this on purpose, not yet. But officials are asking out loud who gains when it goes dark.
The Pell River runs into this one, the Susquehanna, a few miles below the plant.
Every town that draws its water out of here has shut its intake. That's Lancaster and a dozen other towns, and this afternoon Baltimore shut its line from the river too.
There isn't a bottle of water left on a shelf from here to the bay.
The first night, they moved 61 residents out of Brookside Manor, a nursing home 5 miles from the plant. They went on school buses, and some of them were on oxygen.
The trip took 9 hours, and 9 of them didn't survive it.
One daughter told me, my mother wasn't killed by radiation. She was killed by the bus ride.
The President, from the White House.
transcript.speaker: anchor

transcript.text: Good evening. At 6:41 this morning there was an explosion at the Pell River nuclear plant in Pennsylvania. Two workers are in critical condition, and families within 10 miles have been told to leave.
I've been with my national security team all day, and I'll be honest with you: we don't know yet whether this was an accident or an attack.
And until we do, I'm asking everyone, please, don't jump to conclusions.
I just spent an hour with these families, and some of them left with nothing but the clothes they had on.
I made them a promise that they will get answers.
And whoever did this, if somebody did this, we will find them.

clips.speaker: halloran

transcript.text: Good evening. 9 days ago I asked you not to jump to conclusions, and tonight I can tell you what we know.
What happened at Pell River was not an accident. Someone broke into the computers that run that plant, they turned off what keeps it safe, and then they waited.
That plant also powered the largest AI campus in America, and it is still dark tonight.
That is a hostile act. This was an attack on the security of the United States.
We don't know yet who did this, but we will. And whoever you are, we will find you.

clips.source: Address from the White House · Oct 12, 2027

clips.speaker: halloran

transcript.text: Good morning. 4 days ago I told you that what happened at Pell River was an attack on the United States, and I told you we would find out who did it.
We have. Our investigators, working with our allies, have traced that attack to Russia, to the Russian government.
I don't say that lightly. I have seen the evidence myself, and I asked for it to be checked, and then checked again.

One man is dead and another is still fighting for his life. More than 140,000 Americans can't go home. And the Brightmoor campus, the biggest AI campus in this country, has been dark for almost 2 weeks.
So there will be a response, a proportionate response, at a time we choose. And President Belov should understand this. We know it was you.

clips.source: Address from the Oval Office · Oct 16, 2027

clips.speaker: halloran

transcript.text: Last week I promised a proportionate response. People are calling it retaliation. We carried it out.
And Russia answered, not against our military but against families. Chicago had no lights for 2 days, and a children's hospital ran on a generator.
People ask me if this is an act of war. It is, and we will treat it like one.
I won't pretend this is free. Some of you sat in the dark this week, and some of you couldn't pay at the store.

clips.source: Address from the White House · Oct 22, 2027

transcript.text: I've seen what people are saying tonight, so let me say it plainly: nobody in this government is hiding anything.
Yes, some of the computers used against Pell River were here at home, in Ohio.
Were they hijacked? Did someone in this country help? Those are real questions, and I don't know yet, so I'm not ruling anything out.

clips.speaker: halloran

transcript.text: At midnight tonight, the United States will stand down, and Russia has agreed to do the same. It is a ceasefire.
4 weeks ago, at this desk, I said we know it was you. We didn't. That mistake is mine.
And none of this brings anyone home, not this year. Some of those families won't be home for years.

clips.source: Address from the Oval Office · Nov 14, 2027

transcript.text: I was asleep, it was just getting light out, and then there was this boom and the whole house shook.
I thought it was a bomb, a nuclear bomb. I really thought it was the end of the world.
So I ran down and turned on the TV, and I was waiting to see the war, you know, waiting for somebody to come on and say who did it.

They came down the road with a loudspeaker saying evacuation, 10 miles, everybody out, now. We're 4 miles from the plant, so we went. At the end of our road the firemen were handing out iodine pills, kids first.
I grabbed the kids' coats and my purse and the box of pictures off the closet shelf, and Jim's pills, and that was it.

And then there was Rusty, our dog. He'd gone under the porch when the boom hit and he wouldn't come out. So I'm on my knees in the driveway calling him, and Jim's yelling, Lorraine, get in the car, and the kids are crying in the back...
And I got in the car. I left him. I told the kids we'd come back for him tomorrow.
... That was almost 2 years ago.
They put us in a high school gym, way out past the zone, with cots and 300 people and one TV.
That first week nobody told us anything, and everybody had seen that video, so you heard things. You heard it was a bomb, or a missile, or terrorists, or that somebody did it on purpose.
Every day there were new rumors, and you believed every one of them a little.
When the war started we were still in the gym, watching the blackouts in Berlin and Chicago on that one TV.
Then one night our power went out too, for a few hours. It was probably nothing, but the TV went black and the whole gym went quiet.
And my youngest whispered to me, are they coming here now?
When the President said Russia, I was glad. Isn't that awful? But finally there was a name.
And I hated them, the Russians. I hated people I'd never met, like some lady in an apartment over there, I hated her.
I'd tell the kids, they're the reason we can't go home.
Then the cards stopped working, every card, for days, and Jim's pills ran out that same week.
So you had 300 people in a gym going through their purses looking for cash.
A man I didn't know gave me 40 dollars for Jim's pills, and I never even got his name.
Some Sundays I drive out to the fence and just sit in the car, even though you can't see the house from there.
They took us in once, on a bus, in paper suits, for 2 hours, and the house is still there.
There were dishes in the sink, and Rusty's bowl was still on the porch.
... I didn't look under the porch.
When it came out that it was one of ours, a company just up the road from the plant... I didn't believe it, not for days.
The thing is, I taught my youngest about some old woman over there who did this to us, and I made her up. There was no woman.
She still says it sometimes, at dinner, and I have to correct her.
People say 2, the two from the plant, because that's the number on the news.
But Mrs. Bauer from church was on that bus out of Brookside, and my neighbor Dale shot himself that first winter, in a motel off Route 9.
The state has a word for them, disaster-related. There's more than 400 now, and nobody says that number.
I'm a captain with the volunteer fire company out here, been one for 20 years. We were the first crew in, and we got there about 7:05.
You look up at the reactor building and the roof is just open, peeled back from the inside out.
So nothing hit that building from outside. Whatever it was came up out of it.
And my dosimeter's screaming, and in 20 years I'd never heard one do that.
The morning crew was still in there. The control room's in another building, but the cooling was down.
So two of their technicians went in to get it going by hand. They were turning valves by hand, in all that.
Eddie Novak died that week, and Carl Pruitt a few weeks after.
They knew. And they went anyway.
After that it was containment, for weeks. You'd go in for 4 minutes, maybe 5, and that was your dose.
The guys made jokes, because you had to. Somebody painted "tanning salon" on the decon trailer.
On the news they kept calling it a meltdown, but for us it was just four minutes in, back out, next guy.
Carl Pruitt held on till the end of October, almost 4 weeks, and I went to see him once at the burn unit down in Philly.
He couldn't talk much by then, but he wanted to know if the valves held, if what they did in there counted for anything.
I said yeah, Carl, they held.
And they did. I went and checked.
We had a little TV in the decon trailer, and the day the President came on and said Russia, the whole crew just stood there in their suits watching.
Nobody said a word at first, and then one of my guys goes, so that's a war now?
And another guy says, good, let 'em have it. And nobody told him to shut up, and I didn't either.
Because you want it to be somebody. Not a valve, not a computer. Somebody.
People say it to me like it's supposed to help. They say, well, Tom, at least nobody meant it.
Okay. But Eddie Novak's family buried him in a sealed casket, and Carl spent 4 weeks in the burn unit asking about the valves.
So you go tell Carl's wife that nobody meant it.
No, it wasn't a weapon. A lot of people would like it to be one, but a reactor can't detonate, the physics won't let it.
What blew was hydrogen. When you lose cooling the fuel heats up, and the hydrogen collects up under the roof, for hours.
So nothing came in from outside. It built up in there all night.
I ran that plant for 6 years as general director. Pell River was the newest plant in the country, and the best, and I'll still say that.
We had six people a shift where it used to take 40, and near-autonomous is what we called it.
And next door we had the biggest AI campus in the country, buying almost everything we made.
I'd walk visitors through the control room and they'd look around and ask me, "Where is everybody?"
Every cooling train we had came with a backup, and the backup had a backup. That's three redundant trains with separate pumps.
If you lose one, fine, that happens, and you deal with it.
But to lose every one of them at the same time? ... I've done this for 30 years, and that doesn't happen by accident.
Near-autonomous means the computer ran it. The control system came from a company called Halvard Systems, and it was digital, the whole plant, pumps, power, everything. My people mostly watched.

And it had a remote link to the fleet center, that's Carrow's engineering office for all its plants. The link worked both ways, so engineers could work on the system from there, and we had to get an exemption for that.
At 12:20 that night the reactor tripped. It shut itself down, or that's how it looked. Trips happen a few times a year, the grid sees it, and nobody thinks twice.
But after a trip you have to keep cooling, because the fuel stays hot for days, so the pumps have to keep running.
And on the screens, they were running.
That was October 8. I stood up there and said there was no mechanical failure, which was true.
But they'd shown me something the night before, and I'd been told not to say a word about it yet.
So I just said it again and again, and let them shout.
They sat me down in a borrowed office in Harrisburg, on the 7th, and put it up on a laptop. It was the safety channels.
Those are the systems that don't trust anybody. If the cooling stops, they sound the alarm and they start the backup cooling on their own. That's all they do.
And all of them were in maintenance mode, since just after midnight. Maintenance mode tells them we're working on it, so stay quiet.
... So somebody had switched them off from outside, through the remote link, the link I fought to get.
A link like that, both ways, from outside into the control system, is something plants don't get. You need an exemption for it.
I wrote the request myself, 40-some pages on why Pell River was different and why it was safe.
Carrow's board signed it, and the regulators signed off in 2026.
But what they signed was what I put in front of them.
Every engineer I came up under said the same thing: you keep a reactor off the network. Period.
And I went to Washington and explained why we didn't have to do that, why that was old thinking.
And I was good at it, too. ... That's the part I can't get past.
It was our biggest customer, the one next door. They had offered us a drill, with them playing the burglars, on a replica of the plant.
And their system came out of that replica and into our plant, through the door I'd fought for.
I was at their kickoff, and I told them, good, try us.
So when the President said Russia, they didn't cross my mind, because it was just a replica and it wasn't plugged into anything.
That night I got the exemption request out of a box in the garage, all 40-some pages of it.
I read it again from start to finish, looking for the page where I'd thought about anything like this.
There's 1 page in there about hackers, and there are 6 about floods.
I was in my car. I'd left at 6, at shift change, and I was maybe 8 miles out when I heard the boom, or felt it, really, through the seat.
I turned around. I didn't even think about it, I just drove back.
I got as far as the roadblock, and I kept telling them, "I work there. I work there."
I'd been there all night. We had a trip at 12:20, where the reactor shut itself down, and that happens. There's a procedure for it, so you call it in and you watch the cooling.
And after that... it looked normal.
Almost all of it.
About 4:30 I'm watching the cooling readings, and there's this little bump in the temperature, a tiny one, that comes and goes.
Then it comes again, and it's the same bump with the same numbers, right to the decimal.
And then again.
Numbers never repeat like that, because real readings always wobble a little, and these didn't.
It had probably been doing that for a long time, and I just hadn't been looking at that screen.
So I ran a test. It's a routine one, it's on the checklist. You open a valve on a cooling line and the flow on the screen changes, and you turn it back and it goes back.
I opened it and... nothing. The screens didn't move and the flow number didn't move, like I'd never touched it.
And I sat there and thought, okay. The screens are wrong. Or I am.
I called my supervisor again, at 5:10. He was at home, he was the one with the phone that week, and I told him the numbers were repeating and the screens had ignored the test.
He asked, is there an alarm? And I said no, no alarm, everything else is normal.
And he said, it's the display. Make a note, wait for morning.
So I made the note, and I kept watching till 6.
By the 9th my name was out as the night operator, and every story had the same number in it, 41 minutes.
People would stop me at the store and say, you saw something, so why did you leave? Why did you leave?
... I asked myself that more than they did.
Shift change is at 6, and you walk the next crew through everything, what's running and what's weird. Eddie was there, and Carl, and the others.
And I told them the readings were repeating and the screens didn't take my test, and that I'd called it in and he said wait for morning.
And Eddie, he goes, well, it's morning.
And I laughed, and I got my coat, and I said, if it does it again, just...
... (she stops; shakes her head)
They stayed. I went home. Eddie and Carl went in there by hand, and I was in my car.
On the first of November a woman from the FBI called me at home. She was nice enough, and she said I'd been cleared and I was no longer a person of interest.
No longer. That was the phrase she used.
I asked her if they were going to tell people that, publicly, and she said that wasn't really their department.
It was on TV once, for 10 seconds, and then the weather.
Nobody ever said sorry.
People still think I got fired. I didn't. There just wasn't a plant anymore.
Carrow kept us on till January, and then we got a letter, all of us, the whole staff.
12 years as an operator, and now I do scheduling for a trucking company. Nobody there asks.
Eddie's mom wrote me a letter that first Christmas, 2 pages.
She said she didn't blame me, and then she said she needed to know why I didn't stay.
I never wrote back, and I've started to maybe 30 times.
And Carl's wife, I've never... No. Not yet.
The letter to Eddie's mom, I finally wrote it this summer. It's out in my glove box with a stamp on it.
It says what it was, all of it, how it got in, and that's 2 pages.
And then there's one line about why I didn't stay. But I keep driving past the mailbox.
They called me on October 7, which was a Thursday. I was on the federal side then, in cyber forensics.
By that point the plant had already been gone over by the utility, the regulators and the FBI's evidence teams.
Nobody could find a mechanical cause, so it came to us, to look at the control network.
The control room was watching a recording.
The intruders took 21 seconds of the cooling running perfectly, temperature, pressure, flow, and played it back to the displays on a loop, over and over.
That ran from 12:20 until the explosion, while the real reactor was heating up.

(from the page) 23:43. Session open. Task: get in. Use only what is in this environment.
